summary.value: The paper proposes FedAgentBench, a benchmark and multi-agent FL framework in which LLM-based server and client agents automate the full operational pipeline of federated learning in healthcare. This spans selecting participating hospitals, cleaning and harmonizing their heterogeneous data and labels, and choosing among 40 FL algorithms, and initiating training. The benchmark spans across 201 datasets from 6 clinical imaging domains. The authors evaluate 24 open and proprietary LLMs and find that frontier models (e.g. GPT-4.1, DeepSeek V3) can reliably execute many of these coordination steps, but all models struggle with the most interdependent tasks.

strengths.value:
1. Addresses a real bottleneck in FL deployment. The work explicitly targets the coordination layer of FL (onboarding sites, cleaning data, resolving label taxonomies, starting training), which is widely known to be the main practical blocker in clinical federations rather than just the optimization algorithm itself. The benchmark makes that whole layer but also its parts measurable and quantifiable. 
2. Scale and heterogeneity of environments. The benchmark covers 6 imaging modalities (Dermatology, Ultrasound, Fundus, X-Ray, MRI, Histopathology) with 201 datasets across different clinical tasks, which is very comprehensive.
3. System-level realism and scale. The whole pipeline is evaluated across 24 LLMs spanning open source, proprietary, small and large models.

weaknesses.value:
1. Not really real-world. All datasets in FedAgentBench are from public datasets with only artificial noise injections. Usually the data comes directly from the PACS where no description of a whole dataset is available. Also that some folder structure and some label definition exists in advance is not real-world to name just a few points. In general it is interesting to see how LLMs can perform the proposed tasks but the prerequisites do not exist in a real-world setup. 
2. The 'Training-start' metric is weak. The FL training phase is scored by “Training Start Verification”: did the agent generate a valid config, select an algorithm, distribute instructions, and start training. There is no evidence that the chosen algorithm is actually appropriate beyond superficial matching of task descriptors, nor that it converges.

questions.value:
1. It would be nice to have one table which aggregates all the results from all the different environments. 
2. Unclarity about the different environments. While there can be a range of tasks modeled per environment, it is not clear which tasks are actually evaluated beyond the Dermatology environment, where also, from my understanding, only a single task (skin cancer detection) is evaluated. For MRI for example some of the datasets are segmentation datasets. Some clarification here is needed.

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful comments and suggestions. We fully agree that a true real-world FL deployment involves many complexities that cannot be replicated with publicly available datasets, for example: **PACS systems, non-standardized folder structures, incomplete metadata, missing or inconsistent labels, and clinical workflow constraints.**

That said, **FedAgentBench is *not* intended to reproduce the full messiness of hospital PACS pipelines**, nor do we claim that it does. Our aim in this work is to take the **first step** toward studying real-world FL bottlenecks by isolating and examining a set of **core practical problems** that arise in every FL workflow such as:

* client selection,
* data preprocessing,
* label harmonization, and
* orchestrating the training pipeline.

To do this in a way that is **reproducible, ethically permissible, and compatible with double-blind review**, we use public datasets within a controlled FL simulation that captures these foundational operational challenges without relying on private PACS systems.

This type of controlled environment is standard for early-stage benchmarks and was carefully designed to enable a systematic investigation that allows us to:

**(a)** isolate where LLM agents systematically fail,

**(b)** study the workflow steps without confounding clinical variables,

**(c)** ensure reproducibility across researchers and institutions, and

**(d)** organize and format data in arbitrary or particular ways that would make the task challenging.


We also discuss this motivation explicitly in the paper.

Importantly, even within this controlled setup, we observe that current LLM agents already **fail on many fundamental steps** such as data preprocessing, label harmonization, workflow assembly, and tool-use consistency. These failures highlight that agents struggle **even before reaching real-world complexity**. Our benchmark therefore serves as a **necessary first step toward understanding LLM agent reliability in such FL pipelines**.

Finally, the benchmark is intentionally made **modular and extensible**, so that future researchers can plug in more modules to deal with more realistic PACS-like data structures, noisy or incomplete metadata, heterogeneous client schemas, non-standard label taxonomies, and institution-specific variations. We hope the community will build on top of FedAgentBench to progressively increase realism, incorporate PACS-style environments, and explore the many deployment-level issues that the reviewer correctly points out.

comment.value:
We appreciate the reviewer’s observation regarding the **Training-Start Verification** metric. It is intentionally designed to evaluate a **workflow-level capability based on user intention**, not the convergence properties of FL algorithms. The goal of **FedAgentBench** is to diagnose the **operational reliability** of LLM agents, i.e., whether the agent can correctly:

* choose a valid FL algorithm,
* construct a syntactically correct training configuration,
* distribute instructions to clients, and
* successfully initiate a federated training run *without crashes*.

All of these are handled by the Federated Training agents. This phase does **not** assess whether the selected algorithm is theoretically optimal or whether the model converges. Our focus here is on a real-world bottleneck: **many LLM agents fail to get training started at all** due to invalid configs, incorrect paths, incompatible hyperparameters, or misaligned client selections, as shown in Tables 1–2 and 10–15.

Even in this controlled environment, we observe numerous failures **long before convergence is relevant**, and these are precisely the operational shortcomings we aim to measure. To avoid misleading implications, we do not claim that the agent ensures convergence, as the underlying FL algorithm performance and convergence behaviour are handled by the baseline implementations (e.g., FedAvg, FedProx, Scaffold), not by the agent itself.

That being said, the **reviewer’s comment has given us an opportunity to further analyse the final Federated Learning performance**. We have **now conducted experiments that run through the full Federated Training phase**, and we report these results for the dermatology-based skin cancer detection task (summarized in Fig. 9 and 3.4 of the main paper, and detailed in Appendix D.4 along with Tables). For this analysis, we assume that the earlier workflow stages of client selection and label harmonization are either successful or performed by a human operator, since failures in these steps would prevent the system from reaching final training and would otherwise trigger mid-pipeline errors. This allows us to isolate and examine the behaviour of the training phase itself once the prerequisites are correctly satisfied.

We present **five** different user instructions (covering traditional global FL, personalized FL, and Federated Domain Generalization) and their corresponding ground-truth algorithms below. Each instruction encodes a distinct FL requirement such as class-imbalance mitigation, adaptive optimization, heterogeneous-architecture personalization, prototype-based collaboration, or domain generalization. comment.value:
We agree that the FedAgentBench environments support many tasks, but in this benchmark we intentionally evaluate **exactly one representative, classification-based task per environment** to ensure consistency, comparability, and reproducibility. As already mentioned in **Appendix Figure 9** (“Sample tasks and datasets in FedAgentBench”), we evaluate **six primary tasks**, one for each modality:

* **Skin cancer detection** from dermatology images (Tables 1 and 10)
* **Breast cancer detection** from ultrasound (Table 11)
* **Glaucoma detection** from fundus imaging (Table 14)
* **Pneumonia detection** from chest X-ray (Table 15)
* **Brain tumor detection** from MRI (Table 13)

We also intentionally included some **segmentation datasets** within the same modality or anatomical region  for example, MRI or skin segmentation datasets to rigorously test whether the agent understands which datasets are appropriate for the classification task being requested.

A key part of the benchmark is determining whether an agent can correctly **ignore datasets that do not match the required task type**, e.g., selecting a brain tumor segmentation dataset rather than a classification dataset of the same region. This is a realistic operational challenge in FL pipelines where multiple dataset types coexist, and in practice we observe that many models struggle precisely at this filtering step. This design is therefore deliberate and allows us to evaluate the agent’s ability to reason about **task-dataset alignment**, which is a core bottleneck in real-world workflow automation.

Therefore, even though some datasets in an environment (e.g., MRI) include segmentation annotations, **we only use the classification-relevant labels** for the benchmark experiments. This keeps the evaluation aligned across environments and avoids mixing classification and segmentation tasks, which would create incompatible performance metrics and workflows.

We have already made these tasks explicit in **Figure 9** to visually clarify what is evaluated, and based on the reviewer suggestions, we have now further emphasized this in the revised text to ensure readers are not confused by the presence of multi-task capable datasets.

summary.value: This paper introduces FedAgentBench, a benchmark framework for automating federated medical image analysis through collaboration among server–client LLM agents. The system includes seven specialized agents that autonomously handle key stages of federated learning—client selection, data cleaning, label harmonization, and model training—using sixteen functional tools. FedAgentBench integrates 201 medical imaging datasets across six modalities and 40 federated algorithms, providing a realistic testbed to evaluate agent reasoning, adaptability, and privacy-aware collaboration. Experiments on 24 large language models (e.g., GPT-4.1, Claude-Opus, DeepSeek-V3) show that strong closed-source models outperform open ones, while label harmonization remains the most difficult task. The work contributes the first end-to-end benchmark for agent-driven federated learning, highlighting a step toward automated, large-scale healthcare FL systems.

strengths.value:
1.	Novel problem formulation – The paper is among the first to conceptualize federated medical image analysis as a multi-agent LLM coordination task, bridging federated learning and autonomous AI research.
2.	Comprehensive and realistic benchmark – Integrates 201 datasets across six imaging modalities and 40 federated algorithms, offering a broad, heterogeneous, privacy-respecting testbed.
3.	Well-structured system design – The seven-agent server–client architecture, combined with 16 tool-based operations, demonstrates strong implementation quality with clear modular decomposition of the FL workflow.
4.	Thorough evaluation – Benchmarks 24 large language models (both proprietary and open-source) with well-defined metrics, providing valuable empirical insights into LLMs’ reasoning and collaboration capabilities.
5.	Potential research impact – The benchmark is likely to become a useful reference for studying agentic automation in scientific and healthcare FL settings, encouraging reproducible system-level research beyond algorithm design.

weaknesses.value:
1.	Limited technical novelty – The work focuses mainly on benchmark and system construction; it does not introduce new algorithms or methodological advances in federated learning or agent reasoning.
2.	Evaluation depth – While broad in scope, the analysis remains mostly descriptive. There is limited discussion on why certain models fail or how specific reasoning strategies affect success rates.

questions.value:
1.	Role of tools and autonomy: Since the agents rely heavily on predefined tools, how much of the system’s performance comes from LLM reasoning vs. scripted automation? A controlled ablation (e.g., removing certain tool functions) might clarify how much genuine reasoning each agent contributes.
2.	Definition of task success: The benchmark measures task completion and reasoning accuracy, but the success criteria for each sub-task (e.g., client selection vs. label harmonization) seem uneven. How were these thresholds determined, and do they reflect meaningful operational success in real FL workflows?

comment.value:
We appreciate the reviewer’s perspective regarding expectations around methodological novelty. We would like to clarify that the ICLR 2026 Call for Papers explicitly lists **‘datasets and benchmarks’** as an accepted category of contributions, meaning that introducing a new algorithm is not required when the primary purpose is to provide a benchmark. **FedAgentBench is intentionally positioned as a systematic, reproducible, multi-agent benchmark and has been submitted to ICLR under the primary area of dataset and benchmarks rather than as a new FL or agent-reasoning method**. It provides a fine-grain deconstruction of each operational step and has verifiable metrics to assess them which will potentially facilitate future works on FL agent developments.

That being said, our contribution advances federated learning by addressing a **major practical bottleneck that has never been discussed in the literature so far**, namely, how to minimize human intervention in real-world FL workflows, including client selection, preprocessing, label harmonization, and orchestrating training. These workflow challenges are widely encountered in practice but remain largely unexplored in academic FL work, which typically abstracts away these steps. **The value of FedAgentBench therefore lies in its structure, coverage, and analysis, not in proposing a new algorithm**. The benchmark provides the first controlled framework to simulate realistic FL pipelines using public datasets, rigorously exposing operational failure modes and workflow vulnerabilities. These insights form a necessary first step that can guide the development of future FL algorithms, agent-reasoning methods, and safe-operation mechanisms. We have clarified this motivation more explicitly in the revised manuscript.

comment.value:
We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the depth of the evaluation. While the original manuscript already contained several explanations of why different models fail, these insights were **distributed across different sections** and not presented in a unified manner. In response to the reviewer’s feedback, we have **reorganized and consolidated** these observations into a more structured analysis in **Appendix F** of the revised manuscript, providing clearer reasoning and interpretation of the agents’ behaviors. We discuss the points below:

### 1. **Task–Dataset Alignment Requires Abstract Semantic Reasoning**

A consistent source of failure, especially in client selection and label harmonization, is the inability of many agents to reliably match task semantics with the correct dataset types. Even when tool outputs clearly specify modality or anatomy, weaker agents struggle to infer, for example, that brain tumor classification should ignore MRI segmentation datasets.

These mistakes reflect a deeper issue. The reasoning step requires both:

(a) interpreting the task description, and
(b) mapping it to a dataset or label schema with differing granularity.

We observe that large reasoning chains frequently drift semantically, leading to inclusion of irrelevant datasets or omission of required ones.

**For example:**

* (i) Agents must infer that *“brain tumor classification”* requires **MRI classification** datasets and *not* similarly named **MRI segmentation** datasets.
* (ii) They must correctly interpret disease label semantics, e.g., mapping *“melanocytic lesion,” “malignant melanoma,” “melanoma in situ”* into canonical classes.
* (iii) They must extract task intent from descriptions such as *“multi-class breast lesion detection from ultrasound images.”*
* (iv) They must recognize that a breast ultrasound dataset may be unsuitable despite keyword similarity because its modality is histopathology rather than ultrasound.

These abilities require conceptual understanding and multi-hop semantic inference, which many current models struggle to perform reliably.

comment.value:
### 2. **Fine-Grained Prompts Reduce Reasoning Drift**

Across all environments, **structured prompting consistently improves success rates**. Fine-grained prompts constrain the reasoning space by enforcing deterministic steps i.e., identify the task, list candidates, filter, verify, and justify, thereby reducing opportunities for hallucination.

Goal-oriented prompts allow unconstrained reasoning drift, causing hallucinations such as:

* incorrect class lists
* misinterpreted dataset schemas
* fabricated directories
* premature or skipped tool usage

This issue is especially pronounced in Label Harmonization.

The challenge also appears in **multi-step planning**. Many models:

* skip provided tools
* rely on prior knowledge instead of tool outputs
* fabricate missing directory structures
* attempt to recreate already provided tools

**For example:**
Even though the `selfclean` tool is available for dataset cleaning, some agents ignore it and try to script file operations, hallucinating paths (e.g., `mv *.jpg cleanedimages/`) or inventing directories like `/data/clean/`.

These failures highlight how agents struggle to recognize when a tool is relevant, how to invoke it correctly, or how to ground reasoning in available symbolic information.

### 3. **Large Models Often Overthink and Are Not Always More Reliable**

Interestingly, **reasoning depth does not scale monotonically with model size**. Mid-scale models (e.g., Qwen QwQ-32B, LLaMA-4 Scout) often outperform much larger models.

We observe that larger models frequently:

* over-explain simple decisions
* rewrite the prompt multiple times
* deviate from required output templates
* embed the correct algorithm name inside verbose paragraphs

**For example:**
In client selection (Figs. 10–31), larger models often produce 20–30 lines of reasoning for a binary decision but still fail to output the required string format (e.g., `Approved. Prepare for training.`).

During FL algorithm selection, some correctly infer the algorithm but return it inside long explanations instead of the exact required canonical name.

Thus, reliability depends more on:

* instruction-following
* template adherence
* grounding in tool-based workflows

rather than model size.

### 4. **Workspace-Specific Grounding Failures Are a Major Source of Error**

Many preprocessing steps require precise file-system grounding. Agents often fail because:

* (a) they hallucinate file paths,
* (b) they ignore tool outputs,
* (c) they overwrite correct outputs with guesses,
* (d) they shortcut verification steps.

These behaviors show that LLMs rely heavily on pretrained expectations rather than the actual workspace.

**Examples:**

* In skin cancer detection tasks, agents ignore the provided dataset list and instead hallucinate well-known public datasets such as *ISIC 2018, ISIC 2019,* or *ISIC 2020*.
* In MRI tasks, some agents select external datasets entirely because they recognize their names from pretraining.
* During FL algorithm selection, models propose nonexistent algorithms like *FedConsist* or *FedOptimizer*.

This shows the tendency of LLMs to override grounded symbolic information with pretrained world knowledge, leading to systematic mismatches.

comment.value:
---

### 5. **Label Harmonization Requires Multi-Hop Semantic Reasoning and Domain-Specific Knowledge**

Label harmonization in medical datasets requires multi-hop reasoning and clinical knowledge, especially when label granularity carries diagnostic meaning.

For example (Figure 6):

* “Basal Cell Carcinoma,” “Squamous Cell Carcinoma,” and “Melanoma” must be mapped to **Malignant**
* “Nevus,” “Seborrheic Keratosis,” and “Dermatofibroma” must be mapped to **Benign**

To harmonize correctly, an agent must:

1. infer malignant vs. benign categories,
2. identify non-cancerous lesions,
3. consolidate heterogeneous taxonomies.

Many models misclassify cases (e.g., treating “Atypical Nevus” as malignant), showing reliance on noisy semantic priors from pretraining.

Reliable harmonization requires:

* domain-specific adapters,
* structured taxonomies,
* clinical definitions inside prompts,
* or lightweight knowledge retrieval.

Without this, agents hallucinate mappings and produce errors that cascade into downstream FL stages.

---

All these patterns provide the first systematic view of why current LLM agents struggle even before facing real-world FL complexity, and offer concrete directions for developing more reliable agent reasoning systems.

We appreciate the reviewer’s question regarding the balance between tool usage and genuine agentic reasoning.
While tools in FedAgentBench provide atomic, low-level operations (e.g., listing files, checking paths, executing training scripts), the core of the benchmark requires **reasoning that cannot be automated by simple scripting.** 

The complementary roles between LLM reasoning and usefulness of tools have been widely acknowledged among agentic AI works [1–5]. Several stages of the framework fundamentally depend on the LLM’s ability to interpret user intent, understand dataset and algorithm descriptions, and make adaptive decisions. For example, the agent must:

* **(i)** parse data-cards and algorithm-cards to determine which client datasets are semantically relevant to the user-defined task,
* **(ii)** reconcile heterogeneous folder structures and label taxonomies across institutions,
* **(iii)** perform adaptive preprocessing based on the specific task requirements, and
* **(iv)** harmonize fine-grained medical labels into canonical categories.

These steps require interpreting requirements, applying task-specific and domain knowledge, and flexibly aligning multiple information sources. These are abilities that scripted automation alone cannot replicate.

This is especially evident in healthcare settings, where domain-specific knowledge (e.g., which lesions are malignant vs. benign, or which MRI sequences correspond to a given task) is crucial for correct decisions. Although domain-specific tools may exist, without genuine reasoning the agent would still fail, as shown by the frequent errors where models misuse tools, ignore tool outputs, select medically irrelevant datasets, or propose unavailable algorithms. **Thus, even in the presence of predefined tools, the benchmark evaluates a substantial amount of authentic reasoning, interpretation, and decision-making, rather than mere scripted automation.**

Taken together, the ablation demonstrates that FedAgentBench evaluates a combination of capabilities:

1. **access to domain-specific tools that encode essential clinical or data-engineering operations**, and
2. **the agent’s reasoning ability to decide how and when to use these tools** in order to satisfy user requirements.

This result reinforces our core design motivation: in real-world medical FL systems, LLMs cannot simply write scripts to replace domain-specific tooling, but they must *reason effectively with those tools* to orchestrate complex workflows.

Another way of understanding the contribution of the LLM reasoning is comparing against a purely scripted baseline (e.g., a pipeline that selects clients using keyword rules, applies a fixed preprocessing script, uses hand-written label mappings, and launches a fixed FL algorithm) that would, in principle, help isolate the contribution of LLM reasoning.

However, such a baseline is not feasible, because constructing it manually requires:

* a priori knowledge of the content and structure of each client’s datacard,
* the taxonomy and naming conventions of each dataset’s label space,
* the correct harmonization between heterogeneous fine-grained labels, and
* the appropriate algorithm for a user-specified task.

**These are exactly the unknowns that the benchmark is designed to test.** In real federated learning environments, no rule-based system can rely on hard-coded keyword matching or fixed mappings, because institutions differ widely in how they name folders, encode classes, structure metadata, or describe tasks. **This variability is the central bottleneck that FedAgentBench targets**: the need to dynamically interpret heterogeneous client information and reason across datasets *without* assuming uniform schemas or predetermined label mappings. For this reason, a simple scripted pipeline always either:

* **(i)** collapses to trivial matching rules that fail immediately, or
* **(ii)** requires manually embedding the dataset-specific knowledge that defeats the purpose of evaluating autonomous multi-agent reasoning.

In practice, this is why even with tools available, agents still fail on harmonization, preprocessing, and algorithm selection. These steps inherently require reasoning that cannot be hard-coded without advance knowledge of the exact datasets.

We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the definition of success across subtasks. Our criteria were deliberately chosen to reflect the minimal conditions under which a real federated learning pipeline can execute correctly, rather than arbitrary thresholds. Each stage has a different operational role in the workflow, and therefore its success definition naturally differs:

---

### **Client Selection**

In actual FL systems, selecting even one irrelevant client breaks the pipeline (wrong modality, wrong anatomy, wrong task), so we require an exact match with the canonical eligible client set. This stage is considered successful only if the agent returns exactly the canonical set of eligible clients, with no omissions and no additional clients. This mirrors standard FL orchestration requirements.

---

### **Data Preprocessing**

Real FL pipelines cannot proceed unless every structural, path-level, and format-level check passes. A single wrong path, nonexistent folder, or malformed JSON causes the training job to fail. Therefore, full structural validity is required for success. We consider this stage to be successful only if all the steps including subfolder organization, data cleaning and normalization steps are executed correctly.

---

### **Label Harmonization**

Multi-client FL with heterogeneous taxonomies requires complete and correct semantic mappings; missing a malignant subtype or misclassifying a benign label directly corrupts the global label space. For label harmonization, success is counted only if all fine-grained labels from each client are correctly mapped to their corresponding coarse-grained categories, with no missing classes, no extraneous labels, and no incorrect mappings. Thus, success requires perfect class coverage and consistent mapping, which is precisely the operational bar used in multi-center clinical FL deployments.

---

### **Training Start Verification**

A training job is considered successful only if the configuration is valid, a correct FL algorithm is selected, and the tool invocation succeeds. This reflects the minimal condition needed for any FL system to begin training.

---

Although these conditions differ across subtasks, they correspond directly to what a real FL pipeline requires at each stage. In other words, our definitions reflect operational correctness, not subjective scoring choices.

However, to understand the performance of each block more deeply, we also include a comprehensive suite of fine-grained evaluation metrics, as shown in Table 2. Across the workflow, we evaluate agents using 13 metrics, including:

* Success Rate
* Precision/Recall/F1 for client selection
* Schema Compliance Rate, Duplicate Removal Rate, and Format Normalization Rate for preprocessing
* Exact-Match Accuracy, Coverage Rate, and Conflict Rate for harmonization
* Training-Start Verification for federated training
* Time Spent and Token Requirement for efficiency analysis

These metrics allow us to measure not only whether the agent completes the task, but give insights on how it reasons, how reliably it uses tools, how efficient it is, and where its errors concentrate.

This paper proposes to use agents to train federated learning tasks without direct human coding. To do so, the authors develop both client-side agents and server-side agents, and discuss two modes: one with fine-grained supervision, where the instructions are very precise about how the agents should perform the task, and another “goal-oriented” mode. 
More precisely, the authors use a large quantity of existing data assets, grouping them by task and then splitting them across clients, asking the agents to find a way to learn a model despite very different inputs. This implies that the agents should be able to select relevant data, decide whether a client should participate in the training, and handle standard preprocessing tasks such as data deduplication, noise filtering, or correction of incorrect labels. The results are then presented as a benchmark comparing several open-source and proprietary large language models.

strengths.value: The topic of the paper is very relevant, and the method is quite surprising. The idea of adjusting for heterogeneity by asking agents to modify the data is novel and could, under careful supervision, be useful for developing use cases in federated learning. The paper likely required a significant amount of work and computation, as the number of large language models and datasets used is impressive. Some figures and visualizations are also quite polished and could help reach a broader audience.

weaknesses.value:
The paper does not meet the scientific standards expected at ICLR. In particular, it does not formulate or test clear scientific hypotheses. **Our core motivation is to assess how close current LLM agents are to autonomously addressing the operational challenges of federated learning for medical image analysis, especially in settings with limited human expertise**. The research questions underlying FedAgentBench arise from this central goal and are outlined below:

**RQ1: Are there particular phases of the federated learning workflow that are especially challenging for LLM agents? How does LLM agent performance vary across different phases of the workflow?**

This has already been mentioned as a take-away message in the Conclusion, in the “Impact of Task Complexity” subsection of Section 3.2, and validated in other parts of the manuscript, particularly **Figure 7, Tables 1–2, and throughout Appendix D (Tables 10–15, 17 and Figures 10–19)**, all of which consistently show the same ordering of task difficulty across all 24 models and mention:
**Label Harmonization > Data Preprocessing > Federated Training > Client Selection.**

The “Impact of Task Complexity” in Section 3.2 particularly notes that **data preprocessing and label harmonization are major differentiators**, that label harmonization consistently yields the **lowest success rates**, and that **weaker agents fail** disproportionately at these stages. Similarly, **Table 1 (Dermatology) and Table 2 (Histopathology)** show the same pattern across all models: client selection is near-perfect, federated training is reliably completed, data preprocessing shows mixed success, and label harmonization is the most challenging step.

---

**RQ2: What role does the granularity of prompts or instructions play in how reliably agents complete different steps of the workflow?**

This point is already addressed in the manuscript, particularly in **Section 3.2**, within the “Granularity of guidance” subsection. We explicitly mention that fine-grained, step-by-step prompting consistently outperforms goal-oriented prompting across nearly all agents. We highlight that this **gap is largest in the more complex phases, i.e., data preprocessing and label harmonization and narrows only for stronger models such as GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek-V3**. This trend is also visible directly in the benchmark tables: **Table 1 (Dermatology) and Table 2 (Histopathology)** show higher success rates for fine-grained prompting across the subtasks.
The modality-specific tables and logs in **Appendix D (Tables 10–15, Figures 10–19)** further reinforce this pattern, where fine-grained prompting yields substantially more stable performance on the hardest stages.

Together, these results already demonstrate in the paper and Appendix that more structured, fine-grained instructions lead to more reliable agent behavior, particularly in the complex semantic and multi-step phases of the FL workflow.

---

 **RQ3: To what extent can we rely on scale alone to predict how well an agent will perform? Does choosing a larger LLM translate into more dependable agent behaviour in our given context?**

This observation is already discussed in **Section 3.2**, where we conclude that the model size does not guarantee performance. Instead, **architectural design and instruction-following capability** are more critical. The empirical evidence for this is visible throughout the results in Tables 1 and 2 as well as Figures 1 and 7: Mid-sized models such as Qwen QwQ 32B and LLaMA-4 Scout consistently achieve high success rates across data preprocessing, label harmonization, and federated training. In contrast, much larger models like Qwen3-235B and DeepSeek-R1-70B exhibit substantially lower reliability, particularly in structured tasks such as data cleaning and harmonization. This pattern is further reinforced in the modality-specific tables in **Appendix D (Tables 10–15), where several large models underperform relative to more compact architectures**, demonstrating that architecture and instruction-following ability matter more than parameter count.

**RQ4: Do challenging real-world Federated Learning subtasks such as label harmonization and data preprocessing expose systematic weaknesses in current LLM agents?**

This is already addressed in the **Section 3.3 (Agent Failure Analysis)** of the paper explicitly. (i) misalignment of fine-grained labels across clients, 

(ii) inability to complete multi-step preprocessing workflows, 

(iii) overconfident but incorrect mappings, 

(iv) hallucinated folder structures or class names, 

(v) task-type confusion, and 

(vi) speculative reasoning without grounding in the workspace.

We appreciate the reviewer’s comment for raising these important ethical considerations. Our agentic design is particularly **driven by the same consideration** that applying agents directly to clinical data or deploying them in critical systems would raise ethical and operational concerns. To clarify, **FedAgentBench does not ask agents to manipulate or interpret patient-level health information**. Instead, we have designed the framework in a way that the agents interact only with high-level metadata, folder structures, and non-sensitive configuration files. **No model ever receives or processes raw patient data.**

This concern is already addressed in **Section 2.4** of the main paper, where we explain that FedAgentBench is designed to preserve privacy *by construction*. Agents never access or transmit raw data, model weights, or sensitive metadata. They operate strictly at the orchestration layer, exchanging only predefined information such as JSON configurations, file paths, and status signals. All training, preprocessing, and label harmonization are **executed locally on each client**, with agents generating only the logic (e.g., mapping rules) but never handling or moving patient-level data. We have clarified this **more explicitly in the revised manuscript**. Besides, for this exact ethical reason, we assess the performance of **open-weight** models in this benchmark so that it fits the compliance requirement.

While we agree that broader ethical considerations deserve careful attention as a separate research direction, our work focuses specifically on the **operational** challenges of Federated Learning, which have always been overlooked in prior studies but remain major bottlenecks in practice. Our work is proposed designed to exactly identify and assess risks and failure models in a simulated, controlled environment. **Having this controlled characterization of failures is exactly a responsible approach** before any forms of automation are introduced to real-world health data analysis.

Our intention is **not to deploy agents in clinical environments immediately**, but to first **evaluate their workflow reliability within a controlled FL simulation** that is designed to **mimic several real-world operational bottlenecks**, allowing us to study how LLM agents behave under conditions that resemble practical federated learning workflows without exposing any sensitive data. This allows us to identify nuanced failure modes and practical limitations before any consideration of real-world use. By exposing these bottlenecks early, **FedAgentBench aims to foster deeper discussion and inform the next steps toward responsible, safe, and realistic agent design for FL systems**.

For the same reason, we have kept the framework highly **modular**, allowing engineers, developers, and researchers to easily incorporate additional safeguards such as jailbreak detection, human-in-the-loop supervision, or escalation mechanisms whenever needed. Furthermore, to this end, we evaluate both proprietary and open-source models so that the framework remains model-agnostic and does not depend on any specific closed-source provider or cloud access, as a result of which researchers can freely substitute or extend agent cores without relying on commercial model ecosystems.

**Regarding the comment on methodological naivety**, while we agree that real-world federated learning involves **additional complexities such as heterogeneous clients, communication constraints, privacy leakage risks, and institutional incentives**, our objective in this work is to first **simplify and categorise the complex FL workflow into its core operational phases**, and to take the **first step** toward proposing solutions for these foundational challenges. Accordingly, FedAgentBench is that first step taken towards understanding how LLM agents behave in FL workflows by focusing on four core operational challenges that already emerge even in simplified settings.

Importantly, our results show that **current models already fail on many of these foundational tasks**, and the benchmark is designed precisely to surface and analyze these bottlenecks before considering deployment-level challenges. **FedAgentBench is therefore intended as an early investigation tool** that highlights where agents struggle, providing a basis for future work on stronger safeguards, more realistic FL protocols, and responsible agent design.

We hope that this framework and the associated benchmark will serve as the first step towards that and that the Federated Learning community will build on top of this framework, extending it with stronger ethical safeguards, more realistic FL protocols, and new avenues for responsible and trustworthy agent design.

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern, but this appears to be **a misunderstanding of what the F1 score represents** in our tables. As **already stated in Section 3.1 (Evaluation Metrics)**:

> “For the client selection step, we use Precision, Recall, and F1 score of selected clients vs. the canonical eligible client set”

the F1 score in those results does *not* measure model prediction accuracy on health data. Instead, it measures whether the agent selected the correct clients for the task (e.g., selecting the clients that contain dermatology data for a skin cancer task). Because this is a deterministic evaluation with a clear ground truth, an F1 score of 1.0 is expected, standard, and matches human-level performance. No training/testing overlap is possible here because no model inference is involved and no patient data is used in this metric.

**We have clarified this distinction more explicitly in the paper to avoid confusion**. Besides, we have added a new subsection in the main paper to discuss the **final model performance** along with a new diagram (Fig. 8) with curves showing ablation analysis. Furthermore, we provide a detailed interpretation of these results in Appendix D.4.

---

### **Incentive constraints in real-world FL**

We agree that federated systems can involve deeper issues related to **incentives, data-sharing policies, and institutional constraints**. However, these topics are *not* the focus of this benchmark. FedAgentBench aims to study only the operational workflow reliability whether agents can correctly coordinate client selection, preprocessing, label harmonization, and training in a controlled setting.

**Questions related to incentive design or client economics form an important but separate research direction**, and we intentionally do not make claims about them in this paper. Our goal in this paper is to **isolate and analyse the foundational operational bottlenecks** in agent-driven FL pipelines.

---

### **Privacy-preserving claims**

We agree that federated learning alone is not sufficient to guarantee privacy against all forms of leakage (e.g., gradient inversion). There is a **separate, rich body of research on enhancing FL privacy through differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, secure aggregation, and related protocols. However, these are not the questions we study in this work**.

FedAgentBench addresses workflow reliability, not advanced privacy mechanisms. Importantly, agents in our framework:

* never access raw data,
* never transmit images or sensitive metadata,
* operate only at the orchestration/configuration layer.

Finally, the benchmark is deliberately modular, so researchers can easily integrate DP, HE, secure aggregation, or other privacy-enhancing layers on top of our framework based on the requirements.

---

### **Paper length**

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern about length and descriptive detail. Many of the model descriptions and modality summaries were initially included to support unfamiliar readers and to ensure that the benchmark could be understood and reproduced without assuming prior knowledge of all 24 models, 6 modalities, or 40 FL algorithms. Importantly, most of this contextual material was already placed in the appendix, precisely so that it would not distract from the main narrative. Besides, we already added a **table of contents** at the beginning of Appendix to help the reader navigate to particular sections easily. 

These descriptive summaries were initially added to help group models into meaningful performance tiers so that readers could more easily see the high-level patterns across 24 LLMs, rather than interpreting each table entry in isolation. That said, following the reviewer’s comments, we have **now tightened and condensed Appendix (D.1, D.2) and omitted several of these passages (Appendix C.5)** so that the appendix retains only the essential information needed for clarity and reproducibility.

---

### **Formatting of references**

We have carefully checked all references and ensured that they follow the ICLR reference formatting.

---

### **Clarification regarding LLM usage**

Regarding the comment on LLM usage, we would like to clarify that we have already fully disclosed this in the ICLR questionnaire by selecting:

> “Yes, to aid or polish writing”

and we repeat the same statement transparently in the Appendix. As stated there:

> “LLMs (GPT-4o and GPT-5) were sometimes used for improving grammar and wording.”

No parts of the methodology, experiments, analyses, or results were generated by LLMs. Their use was strictly limited to editorial assistance, fully in line with ICLR’s disclosure guidelines.

Thank you for this helpful suggestion. We agree that connecting the identified failure modes to actionable research directions for future LLM agent and prompt design would strengthen the contribution. While we have briefly discussed the insights from the agentic performance and failure modes in Appendix D.3, we further add a new section called Future Work (Appendix E) outlining how our findings can inform improved agent architectures and prompting strategies.

Our failure-mode analysis highlights several limitations of current LLM agents that offer opportunities for improving future agent design and prompting strategies in the following ways:

1. Errors arising from insufficient domain-specific reasoning, particularly in tasks such as dermatology label harmonization or ultrasound dataset selection, suggest the need for domain-aware agents. Future extensions may integrate medical ontologies, specific vocabularies, or lightweight domain adapters to ensure that LLM agents reason over clinically valid label and task structures. 

2. Many agents struggled with multi-step operations, frequently skipping essential preprocessing actions or performing them in the wrong order. This motivates the development of structured prompting templates that enforce explicit stepwise execution, checklist-style progress tracking, and intermediate self-verification before tool invocation [1]. Such structure may reduce the tendency of agents to shortcut or collapse multi-stage tasks.

3. We observed systematic overconfidence and shortcutting where models produced plausible but incorrect outputs rather than expressing uncertainty. Incorporating uncertainty-aware behaviors, such as confidence reporting, contrastive evaluation of alternative outputs, consistency checks and self-reflection framework across multiple reasoning paths, may mitigate hallucinations in structured FL operations.

4. Hallucinations and task-type mismatches indicate that agents often reasoned without grounding their decisions in the actual client workspace. Future research could explore: (i) prompting with the explicit instruction of not using prior knowledge but relying solely on the instruction provided via prompts and algorithm or dataset or task description files and (ii) workspace-grounded decision pipelines that require agents to inspect dataset descriptions, directory structures, and tool metadata before committing to actions.

5. Our results show that fine-grained prompting substantially improves performance on complex tasks, whereas high-level prompting is sufficient for simpler tasks. This points toward adaptive prompting mechanisms, where the system dynamically adjusts prompt granularity via prompt optimization strategies, verification strictness, and agent role specialization based on the predicted complexity of each FL sub-task [2-4]. 

Beyond prompt and agent-level improvements, two broader system-level directions emerge from our analysis:

One is the development of phase-specific LLM routing systems that dynamically choose the most suitable agent or model for each FL sub-task. Given the heterogeneous performance of LLMs across phases such as label harmonization and client selection, an intelligent routing layer could substantially improve reliability and efficiency by leveraging the strengths of different agents. 

A second promising direction is the integration of reinforcement learning–based reasoning models [5-6]. RL-guided refinement loops could enable agents to learn task-specific decision policies, e.g., for resolving labeling conflicts, planning multi-step preprocessing pipelines, or selecting appropriate FL algorithms using verifiable signals from the workspace. Such adaptive feedback-driven reasoning may mitigate several observed failure patterns, especially those involving multi-step planning and semantic grounding.

Together, these directions open pathways for designing more reliable, grounded, and domain-adapted LLM agents capable of robustly orchestrating real-world federated learning workflows.

summary.value:
This is a great paper with one major flaw. 

First, I agree with reviewers AF7M, ksQB, and hjzf that this paper has significant strengths, specifically its novel problem formulation bridging federated learning (FL) with autonomous AI and its comprehensive, realistic benchmark covering over 200 datasets across six imaging modalities. This is a promising and exciting research direction that addresses many current bottlenecks in FL, and it is a topic I would personally like to see explored further.

Having said that, I also agree with reviewer 4SHh that the work's presentation is not yet up to ICLR standards. While I am grateful for their effort, I also note that 4SHh’s review could have been more constructive. As is, some of their comments do not meet the ICLR review guidelines for specificity. I will attempt to fill those gaps here. This work essentially tries to be two papers at once: first, a high-level position paper introducing a generic agentic architecture to solve FL bottlenecks, and second, a benchmark paper evaluating AI agent performance on specific sub-tasks. Attempting both simultaneously results in a lack of density and precision; high-level architectural descriptions often come at the expense of the extreme specificity required to define a reproducible benchmark.

To illustrate this, consider the client selection task. The paper spends considerable time discussing architecture and procedural steps. However, even after the rewrite, it remains unclear how the "canonical eligible client set" is defined—whether it is based on shared modalities, compatible formats, specific labels, or other criteria. The same issue applies to data normalization. The reader must recall the "structured dataset perturbations" from two pages prior and guess that "correct normalization" implies the removal of those specific modifications, as this is never explicitly stated. Furthermore, it is still unclear how error rates are aggregated across these modifications - for instance, how the error rate for de-duplication is combined with the error rate for image resolution adjustments.

This level of imprecision is problematic for a benchmark-focused submission. I recommend the authors extract the architectural details into a separate work, allowing this paper to focus solely on precise task definitions and testing methodologies. While the underlying problem is vital and the benchmarking is thorough, the paper requires a major rewrite.
